'''''Stellaria apetala''''' (syn. ''S. pallida''), '''lesser chickweed''', is an [[annual plant|annual]] [[herbaceous]] [[plant]] in the [[flowering plant]] family [[Caryophyllaceae]]. It occurs in short, sandy grassland by the sea and, less often, in similar habitat inland. It is native to Europe and is well established as an [[introduced species]] worldwide.

==Description==
Lesser chickweed is a low-growing, patch-forming annual herb with a distinctly yellowish-green colour. It has a dense, spreading root mat which makes it difficult to dislodge from the ground. The stems, which are sometimes tinged purple, spread out along the ground without rooting at the nodes, and lengthen to about {{Convert abbreviated|10|cm}} long. They are [[terete]] and [[glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]], with a single line of hairs down one side, which alternates at the nodes. The leaves are opposite, pale green and ovate, 4–7 mm long by 2–3 mm wide, with a pale green or sometimes purple [[hydathode]] at the pointed tip and [[stoma|stomata]] on both sides. The [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] are flattened, hairy and about 3–5 mm long, except at the tip of the stem, where the leaves appear [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]].<ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref><ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>
[[File:Stellaria apetala petals.jpg|thumb|A flower with petals]]
[[File:Stellaria apetala scarious margins.jpg|thumb|The sepals sometimes have a narrow scarious margin towards the tips.]]

Flowering occurs in the early spring, February–May in Northern Europe.<ref name=crib>{{cite book |last1=Rich |first1=T.C.G. |last2=Jermy |first2=A.C. |title=Plant Crib 1998 |date=1998 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London |isbn=0-901-158-28-3}}</ref> The [[inflorescence]]s are terminal and consist of a short [[Cyme (botany)|cyme]] of up to six flowers, which are small, 2–3 mm in diameter. There are four or five hairy oval/lanceolate green sepals 2–3.5 mm long. Most flowers have no petals at all, but a small proportion have five deeply bifid green/scarious petals about 1 mm longer than the sepals, which never open widely. There are usually between one and three [[stamen]]s, sometimes none, with grey-violet [[anther]]s, and three [[Style (botany)|style]]s.<ref name="Stace" /><ref name="Morton">{{cite journal |doi=10.2307/2484204 |last=Morton |first=J. K. |date=March–April 1972 |title=On the occurrence of ''Stellaria pallida'' in North America |journal=Bull. Torrey Bot. Club |publisher=[[Torrey Botanical Society]] |volume=99 |issue=2 |pages=95–103 |jstor=2484204}}</ref>
[[File:Stellaria apetala stamens.jpg|thumb|Flowers typically have three or fewer stamens]]

The fruits are formed a week or two after flowering and consist of an oval green capsule about 3 mm long, which remains surrounded by the sepals. Each fruit contains about 6–8 yellowish-brown disc-shaped seeds which are released when the tip of the fruit opens by six spreading teeth. The seeds are 0.5–0.8 mm in diameter, with a ring of small, blunt [[tubercle]]s around the rim.<ref name="Clapham" /><ref name="efloras">{{cite book | url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242000911 | title=Flora of North America: north of Mexico | publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] | pages=110 }}</ref><ref name="Bojňanský">{{cite book|last1=Bojňanský|first1=Vít|last2=Fargašová|first2=Agáta|title=Atlas of Seeds and Fruits of Central and East-European Flora: The Carpathian Mountains Region|year=2007|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|isbn=978-1-4020-5361-0}}</ref><ref name="Stace" />

''Stellaria apetala'' is [[self-pollinating]] and, because the flowers do not open widely, is often [[cleistogamous]].<ref name="Clapham" />

==Taxonomy==
''Stellaria apetala'' forms part of a complex that also includes ''[[Stellaria media|S. media]]'' and ''[[Stellaria neglecta|S. neglecta]]''.
It was first described by [[Bernardino da Ucria|Ucria]] in 1796.<ref name=powo/> In 1828, [[Barthélemy Charles Joseph Dumortier|Du Mortier]], describing a form found in Belgium, applied the name ''Alsine pallida'', which [[Louis Alexandre Henri Joseph Piré|Piré]] (1863) transferred to the genus ''Stellaria''.<ref name="Whitehead">{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.1967.tb05444.x |last=Whitehead |first=F. H. |author2=R. P. Sinha  |date=October 1967 |title=Taxonomy and Taximetrics of ''Stellaria media'' (L.) Vill., ''S. neglecta'' Weihe and ''S. pallida'' (Dumort.) Pire |journal=New Phytologist |publisher=[[Blackwell Publishing]] |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=769–784 |jstor=2430464|doi-access=  |bibcode=1967NewPh..66..769W }}</ref>

The taxonomic status of ''Stellaria apetala'' <small>(Dumort.) Piré</small> has been confused. Dandy (1958) and Clapham, Tutin and Warburg (1962) adopted the name ''Stellaria pallida''<ref name="Dandy">{{cite book |last1=Dandy |first1=James Edgar |title=List of British Vascular Plants |year=1958 |publisher=British Museum |location=London }}</ref><ref name="Clapham">{{cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=Arthur Roy |author-link1=Arthur Roy Clapham |last2=Tutin |first2=Thomas Gaskell|author-link2= Tom Tutin |last3=Warburg |first3=E F |author-link3 = E. F. Warburg |title=Flora of the British Isles |edition=2nd |year=1962 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=0-521-26962-8}}</ref> but while Clapham et al. treated ''S. apetala'' <small>Ucria</small> as a synonym, Dandy considered this to be a synonym of ''S. media'' <small>L.</small>, as also did Chater and Heywood.<ref name="Chater">{{cite book |last1=Chater |first1=A O |last2=Heywood |first2=V H |author-link2=Vernon Heywood |title=[[Flora Europaea]] |volume=1 |year=1964 |pages=134–135 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-521-08717-1}}</ref> Whitehead and Sinha, having failed to locate any specimens matching the description in the ''[[Flora Europaea]]'', concluded that ''S. apetala'' <small>Ucria</small> or ''S. apetala'' <small>auct.</small> could be regarded as synonyms of ''S. pallida'' <small>(Dumort.) Piré</small>.<ref name="Whitehead" /> ''Stellaria pallida'' is now considered a junior synonym of ''Stellaria apetala''.<ref name=powo>{{Cite web |title=Stellaria apetala Ucria {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:159051-1 |access-date=2022-06-27 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2n = 22.<ref name="Morton" />

The name ''Stellaria'' is from the Latin {{Lang|la|stella}}, for a star, and describes the appearance of the flowers of plants in this genus (not so much this particular species). The prefix "a-" derives from the Ancient Greek, and means "without" or "lacking" and therefore refers to the absence of petals in most specimens. The synonym ''pallida'' comes from the Latin {{Lang|la|pallens}}, {{Lang|la|pallidus}} = pale, and is most likely a reference to the yellowish colour of the foliage.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stearn |first1=William T. |title=Botanical Latin: History, Grammar, Syntax, Terminology and Vocabulary |date=1980 |publisher=David & Charles |location=Newton Abbot |isbn=0-7153-5645-3}}</ref>

==Identification==
Lesser chickweed is easily confused with [[Stellaria media|common chickweed]], especially small plants without petals (''Stellaria media'' var. ''apetala'' <small>Gaudin)</small>. The only certain way to separate them is by a chromosome count, but the following field characters are useful. Lesser chickweed is yellowish, not bright green; the sepals are only up to 3 (not 5) mm long; it has 3 or fewer stamens (''media'' has 3–10); the fruiting capsules are less than 5 mm long; the fruiting pedicels are short and not reflexed; and the ripe seeds are less than 0.9 mm long.<ref name="Morton" /><ref name="Poland" /><ref name=crib>{{cite book |last1=Rich |first1=T.C.G. |last2=Jermy |first2=A.C. |title=Plant Crib 1998 |date=1998 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London |isbn=0-901-158-28-3}}</ref>

==Distribution and status==
''Stellaria apetala'' has a widespread, though local, distribution across Europe, from southern Spain and the Mediterranean islands to [[Sápmi|Lapland]], and from the [[British Isles]] to Ukraine.<ref name="Bojňanský" /><ref>{{cite web | url=http://luirig.altervista.org/schedeit2/pz/stellaria_pallida.htm | title=Stellaria pallida (Dumort.) Pire | access-date=2010-08-13}}</ref> In North America it is found as an [[introduced species]] from [[Ontario]], Canada, to Mexico and throughout the United States, from the east coast ([[Virginia]], [[North Carolina|North]] and [[South Carolina]], and [[Florida]]) to the west coast ([[California]] and [[Washington (U.S. state)|Washington]]).<ref name="efloras" /><ref name="Morton" /> It is also established in many other countries worldwide.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Stellaria apetala Bernardino |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/8311921}}</ref>

In the European Union its threat status has not yet been evaluated,<ref>{{cite web |last1=European Nature Information System |title=Stellaria pallida (Dumort.) Piré |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/167302 |access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref> but in Britain it has been designated [[Least-concern species|Least Concern]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cheffings |first1=C.M. | last2=Farrell |first2=L. |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |date=2005 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
The main habitat for this species is in sandy and gravelly grassland close to the shore.<ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref> It grows on well-drained soils and is able to withstand a fair amount of trampling and grazing. Away from the sea it occurs in sandy areas and is found on woodland rides, waste ground and eroded hillsides. In Europe it is often found growing under the shade of [[Scots Pine]] in woodland on light glacial sands,<ref name="Whitehead" /> whereas in Britain it often occurs in the distinctive [[British National Vegetation Classification|U1 ''Rumex acetosella'' grassland]], where it is sometimes considered an [[axiophyte]] of species-rich habitat.<ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Trueman |first1=I.C. |last2=Poulton |first2=M.W. |last3=Hodder |first3=M.|title=The Flora of Sutton Park |date=2023 |publisher=Pisces Publications |location=Newbury |isbn=978-1-913994-09-9}}</ref>
[[File:Stellaria apetala Perry Wood.jpg|thumb|Lightly trampled woodland rides are a typical habitat.]]

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 7, F = 4, R = 4, N = 4, and S = 0, which signifies a brightly lit situation with dry, somewhat acidic soil, low fertility and no salt.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref>

The flowers are [[Cleistogamy|cleistogamous]] and are not visited by pollinating insects. The UK's Database of Insects and their Food Plants lists no species that feed on lesser chickweed, although there are several [[Fly|Diptera]] and other insects which are known to attack chickweeds (''[[Stellaria]]'' spp.) generally.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pitkin |first1=B. |last2=Ellis |first2=W. |last3=Plant |first3=C. |last4=Edmunds |first4=R. |title=The leaf and stem mines of British flies and other insects |url=http://www.ukflymines.co.uk/Keys/STELLARIA.php}}</ref>

Two species of fungi have been recorded on lesser chickweed in Europe: [[Peronospora|Peronospora alsinearum]] is a downy mildew and ''[[Puccinia arenariae]]'' creates pustules on the leaves.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ellis |first=Willem |title=Stellaria pallida |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/en/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superasterids/caryophyllales/caryophyllaceae/alsinoideae/alsineae/stellaria/stellaria-pallida/ |access-date=6 May 2026 |website=Plant Parasites of Europe}}</ref>
